news.title: Springville Once Supplied Iron Ore to Three States
news.summary: An 1880 census lists a likely Springville-area mine producing 12,085 tons of iron ore. Where did the ore go, why did mining decline, and could some of that iron have returned as the cast-iron storefront on Main Street?
body: Could the iron columns on the old Presley Store have started out as rock dug from one of the mountains overlooking Springville? We do not know, but the dates and the routes taken by our ore make the question worth asking. Long before the store opened in 1902, Springville was shipping iron ore to furnaces in other states.

The ore was already there when the Alabama and Chattanooga Railroad reached Springville in 1870. What changed was the cost of getting it to a customer. A railroad could carry quantities of rock that would have been impractical to move long distances by wagon.

Local historical records place A. W. Woodall in the mining business by 1877. He employed both Black and white laborers and by 1880 was selling to James W. Sloss and Henry DeBardeleben, two men central to Birmingham’s industrial growth. Around 1900, Woodall built an ore tram across Talladega Street. For those of us who drive through town today, it is remarkable to think of a tram carrying ore across a street we still use.

David A. Aderholt's 1904 biography describes him as an early participant in sending regional iron ore to Tennessee and an organizer of Spring Lake College. The mining survey spells a landowner's name A. D. Aderholt; we have not established whether that was the same man. Either way, the Aderholt name connects two fascinating strands of local history.

The 1880 census recorded 12,085 short tons at Hugh Carlisle’s St. Clair County operation. The directory calls the location 'Near Springfield'; a trade journal in 1889 places Carlisle's formerly large operation near Springville. Taken together, the records strongly suggest the same local enterprise. If so, Carlisle's operation ranked sixth by reported tonnage among the 29 Alabama entries on the census page. That is not a ranking of towns or a complete accounting of Springville's mines.

The census also records Carlisle's customers as the Southern States Coal, Iron and Land Company and the Rising Fawn furnace in Georgia. Its entry for the Rising Fawn operation on the following page identifies such uses as stoves, machinery, bar iron and nails. Those are products associated with that operation, not proof that our particular ore went into any one of them.

The furnaces turned ore into pig iron, which could then be refined or remelted to manufacture other products. One interesting possibility is South Pittsburg, which later became home to Lodge Cast Iron. We know ore from our area went to that town, but we have no evidence that a Lodge skillet contains Springville iron.

The most useful discovery is a federal survey made for the 1880 census. It describes the rock, its iron content and even the original land-survey sections. Woodall had a small abandoned tunnel in one section and active surface mining in another. The survey also describes an Aderholt opening four miles northeast of town. Figure 159 illustrates its soft red ore changing to harder bluish limestone below a fault.

The survey measured one Woodall sample at 53.28% metallic iron. Another sample from the same property measured 49.49%. The Aderholt stockpile beside the railroad yielded 48.40%. Those figures help explain why the ore attracted buyers.

A 1910 report describes a prospect 2½ miles northwest of Springville and additional workings along the ridge northeast of town. At a site 1½ miles north of the former St. Clair railroad switch, miners had reportedly produced 12,000–15,000 tons over roughly two years; some underground passages ran 50–200 feet. That reported tonnage is separate from Carlisle’s census figure and should not be added to it without establishing whether operations overlapped.

The township and section descriptions give us a starting point for matching the old workings with present-day land records. We have not yet confirmed current surface owners, mineral-rights holders or which workings remain visible. A tax parcel map alone would not establish mineral ownership.

A striking observation in the February 7, 1889 issue of The Iron Age says that Carlisle had once conducted substantial operations near town, but that despite the abundance and quality of the ore, 'no work is now done there.' This was a snapshot of conditions in 1889, not proof that all local mining had ended. Woodall’s later tram suggests otherwise.

The 1910 USGS report still regarded the area northeast of Springville as a potential source of ore. Its surveyors described folds, changes in the angle of the beds and a nearby fault. A mine might have promising rock at the surface without being able to follow that same ore efficiently underground.

Think about the difference from a miner’s perspective. A thicker seam potentially offers far more ore for the same length of excavation. Birmingham also had major furnace companies controlling mines, coal and transportation close to their plants. It is plausible that the economics of competing against them became unfavorable for smaller suppliers, even if Springville still had good ore. No surviving record we have located establishes the exact reason or final date for the closure of our local mines.

The town's businesses continued to diversify. Goodwin’s Mill opened on Canoe Creek around 1900, grinding grain, and Bob Ewing established a cotton gin in 1902. Stores and a bank helped serve surrounding farms. Agriculture, processing and trade overlapped with mining rather than abruptly replacing it on a known date.

The Presley brothers opened their general store at 601 Main Street in 1902. Its cast-iron storefront is still a rare feature in St. Clair County. The original 1982 preservation nomination identifies the builder or architect as unknown and does not identify the foundry that produced the ironwork.

Imagine ore leaving Springville by rail, being smelted and eventually returning as the decorative columns on a building downtown. It is a plausible route for iron in that era, but there is no evidence yet linking our mines to those columns. The iron could just as easily have been cast elsewhere from unrelated ore, scrap or a mixture of sources.

A foundry stamp on a column or a surviving invoice from the Presley family might help trace the manufacturer. Even finding the foundry would not necessarily reveal where it purchased its raw materials. If you know where the old tram ran, have family photographs of the mining operation or have seen a manufacturer's mark on the Presley storefront, we would love to hear from you.

news.title: Springville Once Attracted Visitors With Giant Carp
news.summary: Mayor James McLaughlin stocked Springville’s former lake with carp that grew large enough to become a local attraction. By the 1950s, families traveling through town were stopping to feed the fish by hand.
body: Jerry C. Smith recalls feeding the fish during childhood trips in this illustrated account of Springville Lake.

news.title: Springville Once Had Its Own College
news.summary: Spring Lake College once drew students to Springville from as far away as Texas. Some boarded with local families in the early 1900s.
body: Discover St. Clair explores the college and the town's history through the recollections of local residents.

news.title: Springville Has St. Clair County's Only Cast-Iron Storefront
news.summary: Did you know the Presley Store at 601 Main Street has the only cast-iron storefront in St. Clair County? Built in 1902 for brothers Porter and John Presley, it's a one-of-a-kind part of downtown Springville.
body: Explore the Presley Store's history and photograph on Wikipedia.

news.title: Summer Readers Grow More Than 3,200%
news.summary: When Jamie Twente arrived in 2015, Springville Public Library's previous summer reading record was just 25. In 2026, participation reached 829—more than 3,200% above that earlier mark. A remarkable achievement for Twente and the library team.
body: Read The Trussville Tribune's original report for the story behind the library's success.

news.title: Springville's downtown is a nationally recognized historic district
news.summary: Springville's historic district joined the National Register of Historic Places on July 3, 1997, recognizing the architecture and history of its old downtown.
body: Did you know Springville has a historic district recognized by the National Park Service? The Springville Historic District was added to the National Register of Historic Places on July 3, 1997.

The federal listing identifies architecture, commerce and social history as reasons the area matters. Its documented architectural styles include Late Victorian, Queen Anne and Early Commercial, reflecting how Springville developed as a railroad-era trading town.

The district covers part of the historic downtown around streets such as Academy, Wilson and Cross. The recognition helps tell the story of buildings and neighborhoods residents still encounter today.
news.sourceName: National Park Service · National Register of Historic Places

news.title: The night a train explosion shook Springville
news.shortTitle: A Train Derailment Set Off Explosions
news.summary: On January 16, 1969, a train derailed at the Springville Depot. Its cars struck propane tanks, setting off explosions and a fire.
body: On January 16, 1969, a train derailed at the Springville Depot. Its cars struck propane tanks, setting off explosions and a fire.
Firefighters came from as far away as Birmingham, and the National Guard joined the response. Buildings were damaged, but no one was killed.

news.title: When Springville was Pinkhill
news.summary: For a brief time in the 1830s, a letter bound for what is now Springville could be addressed to Pinkhill.
body: The settlement’s earlier name was Big Springs. Fresh water made it a stopping place for Native Americans and, later, settlers traveling through the area. When the first post office opened in 1833, the name on the mail was Pinkhill.

Pinkhill had a short run. In December 1834 the name changed to Springville, bringing the springs back into the town’s name. Of the town’s three names, two point to the water that first drew people here.

news.title: Springville's Charlie Hare signs with Gadsden State
news.summary: Springville High School senior Charlie Hare signed to play baseball for Gadsden State, with one more season ahead for the Tigers.
body: Springville High School center fielder Charlie Hare signed his letter of intent on Nov. 12 to play college baseball for the Gadsden State Cardinals, according to a Nov. 17 report in The Trussville Tribune.
Hare's junior season was cut short by injury. Before then he was batting .375 with a .460 on-base percentage. He plans to return for one more Tigers season, expected to begin in March.

news.title: New Springville art gallery planned for Highway 11
news.summary: Dibble Dabble Art Gallery announced a Nov. 12 opening at 6441 U.S. Highway 11, with art by local and central Alabama artists.
body: Dibble Dabble Art Gallery announced a grand opening and ribbon cutting for Nov. 12 at 6441 U.S. Highway 11 in Springville, according to a Nov. 11 report by The Trussville Tribune.

The opening-day schedule included a glassblowing event and an evening open house. The gallery was described as a place to see work by local and central Alabama artists. Check with the gallery directly for current visiting hours.
